Empirical Research Plan: Immigration → Native Labor-Market Outcomes

────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy
Strategy chosen: shift-share instrumental‐variables (Bartik-type) difference-in-differences at the education × experience (skill-cell) level, optionally interacted with regions.

Rationale  
• The key endogenous regressor—the contemporaneous immigrant share in a native skill group—is plausibly correlated with unobserved labor-demand shocks (immigrants move to booming cells), so OLS is biased.  
• A shift-share IV exploits (i) the historically different propensity of each skill cell to employ immigrants (“shares”) and (ii) country-wide or origin-specific shocks that change total immigration (“shifts”). The interaction generates quasi-random variation in immigrant inflows that is arguably orthogonal to contemporaneous cell-specific labor-demand shocks.  
• With two or more years the design is equivalent to a DiD: skill-cells with high pre-1990 immigrant shares receive a larger “treatment dose” after, say, 1990–2000.  
• The method can be implemented uniformly in the U.S. (Census/ACS 1990–2010), U.K. (LFS 1995–2005), and Germany (IAB 1990–2000) and aggregates easily to education-experience-by-region cells to allow country-specific robustness checks.

2. Treatment and Control
Treatment variable  
∆ImmShare_ct  = change in the immigrant share in cell c between t-1 and t (or the level in cross-section regressions). Main outcome: ∆log wage_ct or ∆employment-rate_ct of natives.

Instrument (Z_ct)  
Predicted immigrant inflow using 1980 (U.S.), 1991 (U.K.), or 1987 (Ger.) cell-by-origin shares:  
Z_ct = Σ_o ( Imm_co1980 / Pop_c1980 ) × ∆Imm_ot ,  
where ∆Imm_ot is the national inflow of immigrants from origin o between t-1 and t.  

Control group / counterfactual  
Cells with low historical immigrant exposure serve as implicit controls; treatment “intensity” varies continuously. Because estimation includes cell and period fixed effects, identification comes from differential changes within a country over time.

Treatment timing  
U.S.: 1990–2000, 2000–2010; U.K.: 1995–2000, 2000–2005 (pre- vs. post-EU enlargement); Germany: 1990–1995, 1995–2000.

No RDD, so no running variable.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
A1. Relevance: skill-cells with larger historical immigrant shares receive larger predicted inflows (first-stage F ≫ 10). Highly plausible given persistence in country-of-origin clustering by education/experience.

A2. Exclusion: national origin-specific inflows (the “shifts”) are not driven by contemporaneous shocks to a particular host-country skill cell’s labor demand after controlling for country-year fixed effects. Plausible: wars, exchange-rate changes, and policy reforms in origin countries drive aggregate inflows; still, cannot rule out endogenous demand pull.

A3. Stable shares: pre-period immigrant shares are measured before outcome shocks; they must be predetermined. Using 10-year lagged shares limits feedback.

A4. No differential native out-migration correlated with predicted immigrant inflows conditional on controls. Plausible in short panels; can be probed by estimating native mobility responses.

A5. SUTVA/partial equilibrium: immigrant inflow to one skill cell does not directly change wages in another cell except through our equilibrium channel captured in the regression. We can relax this by estimating cross-skill spillovers.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
T1. Endogenous origin-specific inflows correlated with macro demand (e.g., business cycles).  
Mitigation: control for period fixed effects, interact with country-level unemployment, or instrument further using exogenous shocks (e.g., political refugee waves, distance × conflict).

T2. Native sorting across regions/industries/skills in response to anticipated immigrant inflows.  
Mitigation: estimate elasticities using cell-by-state fixed effects; test pre-trends; instrument shares in t with inflows in t + 1 to check anticipation.

T3. Measurement error in education/experience downgrading blurs skill-cell assignment.  
Mitigation: create alternative cell definitions (broad vs. narrow), re-run regressions; use occupation-based skill classification as robustness.

5. R Code Outline
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ivreg)   # for 2SLS diagnostics

# 1. Load data (example: U.S.)
us <- fread("US_Census_skillcells_1990_2010.csv")  # cell-level panel

# 2. Variable construction
us[, imm_share  := immigrants / (immigrants + natives)]
us[, native_wage:= total_native_wage / native_workers]
us[, lwn        := log(native_wage)]

# Change over decade
us <- us[order(cell, year)]
us[, d_imm      := imm_share - shift(imm_share), by=cell]
us[, d_lwn      := lwn - shift(lwn),             by=cell]

# 3. Build shift-share instrument
# Step 1: baseline shares in 1980 (or first year)
base <- us[year==1990, .(cell, origin, base_share = immigrants / sum(immigrants)), by=origin]
# Step 2: national inflows by origin
nat <- us[, .(nat_inflow = sum(immigrants)), by=.(origin, year)]
nat[, d_nat_inflow := nat_inflow - shift(nat_inflow), by=origin]

# Merge to compute predicted inflow
shiftshare <- merge(base, nat, by="origin", allow.cartesian=TRUE)
shiftshare[, Z := base_share * d_nat_inflow]
Z_ct <- shiftshare[, .(Z = sum(Z)), by=.(cell, year)]

us <- merge(us, Z_ct, by=c("cell", "year"))

# 4. Main 2SLS regression
mod <- feols(d_lwn ~ 1 | cell + year | (d_imm ~ Z), data=us, 
             cluster="cell")
summary(mod)

# 5. Robustness: leave-one-origin-out instrument
big_origin <- "Mexico"
Z_lo <- shiftshare[origin!=big_origin, .(Z_lo = sum(base_share * d_nat_inflow)),
                   by=.(cell, year)]
us <- merge(us, Z_lo, by=c("cell","year"), all.x=TRUE)

robust_mod <- feols(d_lwn ~ 1 | cell + year | (d_imm ~ Z_lo), data=us,
                    cluster="cell")
etable(mod, robust_mod, se="cluster")

```

6. Expected Results
Theory (nested CES model with imperfect substitution) predicts:  
• Within skill groups directly “competing” with immigrants (e.g., low-educated, 0–20 yrs exp.), elasticity of native wages w.r.t. immigrant share roughly −0.3 to −0.1.  
• For high-skill natives, effect may be zero or even positive due to complementarity.  
• Aggregate native wages/employment likely close to zero; any losses at the bottom are partly offset by gains at the top.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV version)  
C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F>10) .................. 1  
C2: Exclusion from skill-cell demand shocks .................. 0.5  
C3: No endogenous native mobility across skill-cells ......... 0.5  
C4: Measurement of treatment/outcome accurate ............... 0.8  
C5: No violation of SUTVA/cross-cell spillovers .............. 0.5  

Total ≈ 3.3/5 → acceptable but demands extensive robustness and falsification tests.

────────────────────────────────────────
